text: LGBTQ issues. In the 2018 cohort, not a single Republican or conservative winner could be found among the biographies. Most recently, for the class of 2025, we found 43 of the 54 winners have worked for Democratic politicians, advocated progressive causes, or identify as left-leaning. Only three scholars openly supported conservative causes. The College Fix also reviewed the jobs and careers of the 2015 to 2022 cohorts to determine what the Truman beneficiaries are doing now. Our research revealed that the scholarship spawns 35 Democratic careers for every one Republican career. At least 226 of these scholarship recipients have obtained jobs and careers directly tied to or advancing left-wing beliefs or the Democratic platform. In contrast, only four Truman alumni could be found to have worked in GOP politics or conservative causes. The Truman Scholarship also seeks regional diversity in its selections and tries to award its scholarships to students from winners in every state. We looked at the 125 Truman Scholars from 2015 to 2024 from states like Georgia, Florida, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, and Utah. Of those, 60 of the scholars, or 48%, went to have at least one job working for left-wing, progressive, or Democratic causes after winning the scholarship. In contrast, only three winners could be found to have gone on to work for a conservative or Republican cause. The imbalance shows that those nominating and selecting the winners of this taxpayer-funded scholarship favor left-wing, Democratic, and progressive causes. This structural bias persists across many years, and it contradicts the program's public purpose. The decade-long data reveals a taxpayer-funded program that, in practice, functions as a talent pipeline for the Democratic Party and liberal activist organizations. Thank you. I look forward to our discussion today. Thank you. And now I recognize Ms. Harrington for your testimony.

morning, Chairman Owens, Ranking Member Adams, and members of the subcommittee. My name is Ashley Harrington. I serve as a senior policy counsel at the Legal Defense and Educational Fund. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. Founded by our nation's first Black US Supreme Court justice, Thurgood Marshall, LDF is America's premier legal organization fighting for racial justice. For 85 years, LDF has advocated for equal opportunity for all. We work to dismantle barriers that hold people back because of their race, their ZIP code, or the wealth they were born into. Since the historic US Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Board of Education, which LDF litigated and won, we have continued to fight for the rights of Black students to receive high-quality, equitable educational opportunities as guaranteed by the 14th Amendment. Our constitutional principle of equal protection under the law mandates that school districts, post-secondary institutions, states, and the federal government provide equal educational opportunities for all students, including Black students and other students of color, LGBTQIA students, students with disabilities, immigrant students, and other historically marginalized populations. Today's hearing is about the Truman Scholarship, which was created by Congress 50 years ago to invest in future public servants. The bipartisan board of trustees that oversees the Truman Scholarship and the individuals involved in selecting scholars have recognized potential for impactful public service in roughly 3,500 talented individuals over the past half century. These scholars are selected without regard to partisan identity and pursue varied fields of study, ranging from law and policy to public health and education. Attempts to label broad categories of public service as inherently partisan are harmful. But we know what this is. This is just the latest action in the continuous effort of the Trump administration and its congressional allies to infringe upon the First Amendment rights of individuals by attempting to punish those who disagree with the administration's ideologies. But public service has no ideology, and public service certainly cannot be cabined only to those views and issues that the administration favors. Regardless, the Truman Scholarship represents an appropriation of $3 million a year and directly impacts just 50 to 60 students annually. The cuts to the higher education safety net made in the One Big Beautiful Bill are of far greater consequence to the millions of Americans who have never even heard of the Truman Scholarship. They are the students who are already struggling with student debt, the parents unsure how they will pay for their children's education, and the working adults trying to return to school to improve their lives. Every year, millions of students enroll in college, and millions more pursue graduate and professional degrees. They do so because they understand the earnings premium and opportunities that come with education, but they also do so with growing anxiety about affordability, debt, and whether our systems are truly designed to support them. They include students of color, first-generation students, veterans, adult learners, and low-income Americans, current and future students who are counting on this committee to care about their economic mobility and their access to opportunity, not just talking points. The Truman Scholarship's $3 million is a drop in the bucket compared to what our nation spends on higher education each year. Across programs and departments, we spend hundreds of billions of dollars every year on higher education, with about $120 billion allocated to students in federal grants and loans alone. There are 43 million Americans shouldering $1.6 trillion in student debt. That is why I hope today's conversation can shift towards making our entire higher education system more affordable and accessible for all students, instead of having a narrow, partisan dialogue about the very few who receive this elite scholarship. Instead of removing barriers, the OBBB constructs new ones, pitting everyday Americans against the wealthy few and making it even harder for people to pursue education as a pathway to a better life. But there is another way. Congress can increase the Pell Grant, invest in historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions such as predominantly Black institutions. They can ensure that grad students and dependent students have access to the aid needed to pursue higher education, ensure that there are truly affordable repayment options for student borrowers that include pathways to debt relief. They can strengthen protections against predatory institutions, and they can protect the Department of Education, because none of this is possible unless it is fully resourced to enforce civil rights, administer aid, and oversee institutions. The pursuit of racial justice and equal opportunity for all should be a shared value and not exclusive to a single party. Students and families deserve more from their policymakers. They deserve a higher education system that opens doors rather than closes them, and a Congress committed to ensuring that opportunity is not reserved for the privileged, but available to all. Thank you.
Thank you so much. I'd last like to recognize Mr. Kissel for your testimony.

Thank you, Chairman Owens, Ranking Member Adams, and members of the committee. My name is Adam Kissel. I am a visiting fellow for higher education reform at the Heritage Foundation. The views I express today are my own and should not be construed as representing Heritage. I also was Deputy Assistant Secretary for Higher Education Programs at the Education Department in the first Trump administration. Thank you for this opportunity to outline some ideological biases in the structure and rhetoric of the Truman program, and I'll offer two ideas for addressing them. First, the program steers applications to the left and discourages applications from the right. Just look at the website. The sample application responses have several examples. No example of a successful response is right-coded, while many are clearly left-coded. Topics for the successful essays included environmental racism and community organizing, while unsuccessful ones included students who wanted to study military history, students who are Christians, students who express patriotism. Second, the website directs advisors of applicants to focus on, quote, "change agents." This term is commonly used on the progressive left due to its ideology of radically changing American institutions. Likewise, the program privileges, quote, "advocacy" over other kinds of public service. You can see this for yourself on the website. This rhetoric discourages conservatives from applying because we often more— more often speak of preserving American traditions and values. For us, public service often means supporting what is good in the current order against efforts to change it. Third, the program's regulatory definition of public service—getting into some details here, it's not in the statute—this definition is also somewhat left-coded. The definition emphasizes environmentalism, but not, for example, protection of unborn children. Imagine who would apply if the program instead gave examples of constitutionalists or promoters of strong families or federalism. Fourth, the program excludes MBAs almost entirely from the competition. The positive role of American business in society might be something we'll have to debate another day, but even the left today recognizes how profit-making businesses engage in public service in many ways. This MBA prohibition, again, is not in the statute or regulations; it's just in the operation of the program. And finally, higher education is skewed deeply to the left, so the applicant pool itself is skewed deeply to the left. So no one should be surprised that right-leaning colleges seldom see the point of sending applicants. Pepperdine, Liberty, Grand Canyon universities, they've had zero Truman Scholars across the program's entire history. Hillsdale has had just one. So I have two policy ideas or recommendations to consider. Easy one, as Mr. Hess said, is revise the program's regulations and website to remove their biases, including the definition of public service, so that it's as neutral as it can be, not discouraging conservatives or or any ideology. And second, an idea to consider is to harmonize the Truman program with a program called the Graduate Assistance in Areas of National Need program, GAANN. In that program, the Secretary of Education consults with other agencies and nonprofits, say the National Science Foundation, Department of War, to determine the national need in graduate education. And this process results in priorities that genuinely serve the nation, such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and this is under both Republican and Democratic administrations for the GAANN program. These changes would better honor President Truman's legacy. So thank you again for the opportunity to provide this testimony.

Thank you. Thank you so much. Under committee rule 9, I will now question the witnesses under the 5-minute rule. I will recognize myself for 5 minutes. Dr. Hess, you mentioned that students interested in the four prominent left-leaning issues outnumber those interested in the four prominent right-leaning issues by better than 12 to 1. That's truly unbelievable, by the way. If the tables were turned and liberal students were being discriminated against, the left would be irate. Are you aware of any federal education programs where conservatives win 12 times as much as liberals?

No, I am not. And I think it's important to understand here that this is not just about partisan balance. The point of the Truman is to recruit young Americans who are interested in public service so that they might advance, so that they might serve the needs of the nation. This is about Americans who bring different values and different ideas to the table.

Thank you. I think we all can agree, and I'm going to ask Ms. Harrington a quick question, that any taxpayer funding should be—opportunities should not be discriminatory. Correct, right? Anything that taxpayers are paying for should not be discriminatory. That's easy. Yes or no? Yes. Okay, thank you. There are millions and millions of Black conservatives like myself. How many Black conservatives have ever been selected as Truman Scholar?
Sorry, is that to me, sir?
Yes.

I don't think any of us know. Right. Even the research that we're talking about today has only looked at a limited number of bios, and they're doing it based on their own research of social media. And, and not having— there's no way to

find out if this— if this— In other words, we're trying to make sure that it is very open, very inclusive, and there's no way to see if any Black conservatives ever have been selected as Truman. That should be a big deal. I would think that would be a really highlight of the Truman Scholarship Program to say we service everyone, including Black conservatives.

I think the bigger deal is, does our higher education system as a whole service everyone? And what we're worried about are the millions of Americans, not the 50 or 60 a year. There are millions of Americans struggling in our higher education. And

We're losing that battle, by the way, because of liberal policy. All right. Thank you so much. Ms. Kabbany, you mentioned The College Fix has been investigating Truman Foundation for nearly 10 years. One thing that struck out to me is how consistent your finding are each year. Liberal winners massively outnumber conservatives every single year, regardless of which party is in power, who's running in office. What do you think this says about the program itself? Well, what it says is that this program is essentially a talent pipeline and taxpayer-funded scholarship program for the Democratic Party and the liberal activist network. It also shows that the system is inherently broken. There's a systemic bias that starts at the campus level all the way up to the final decisions that needs to be reformed. Thank you. Miss Kissel Mr. Kissel, you mentioned the program structure assumes that for-profit corporations in the private sector can never serve the public, and conversely, nonprofits, the government sector, always act in the public interest. Personally, I don't think either of this is true. Can you say more about why some types of for-profit work perhaps could count towards Truman Public Service requirements?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Uh, whenever there's a voluntary transaction, both sides are better off. That's Econ 101. When any public company, uh, or, or for-profit company is contributing to the public by selling goods and services that people want, they're engaging in a kind of public service. But maybe more to the point, lots of companies have a public service component to what they do. They'll have a philanthropy arm, they'll have a community outreach arm. And if you are in a field where you're helping the public, it shouldn't matter whether the structure of your organization is for-profit or nonprofit.
Thank you. Okay, I'm going to yield back my time now to the ranking member, recognize for the purpose of questions and witnesses.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. When students dream about college, they shouldn't be left wondering whether the federal government will still be there when they arrive, wondering if the Department of Education will be open or wondering if the programs they rely on—Pell Grants, campus support programs, HBCU funding—will still exist by the time they graduate. I spent more than 40 years in the classroom as a professor, and I know that uncertainty by itself can derail a student. When programs disappear overnight, students lose their footing, and when an entire federal program is put on the chopping block, the consequences are felt in in every classroom, every campus, and every community. So let's put the numbers in perspective. The Truman Foundation is receiving a lot of attention today, but students aren't struggling because of the Truman Scholarship. They're struggling because Congress passed a law that gutted Pell, slashed student aid, and weakened the support systems that help low-income and first-generation students stay enrolled. And while we debate a scholarship program that has supported public service for nearly 50 years, we're watching in real time the federal government dismantle the U.S. Department of Education. The Trump administration has laid off nearly half of the department's workforce, it's canceled and withheld billions in grants, and it's signed interagency agreements to move critical functions, including the entire Office of Postsecondary Education, out of the department altogether. Well, that's not reform. That is a retreat from our responsibility to students. So let me turn to our witnesses. Ms. Harrington, the Truman Foundation could receive roughly $30 million in federal support over 10 years, but H.R. 1, which my colleagues supported, cut $284 billion from education over that same period. So can you speak to the relative importance of that $30 million compared to the scale of the $284 billion in cuts? And what does that difference mean for students, for institutions, for the future of federal support for higher education?

Absolutely. It's a drop in the bucket. The billions of dollars, hundreds of billions of dollars that we spend every year, the hundreds of billions of dollars that are going to be cut because of this bill are going to, those cuts are going to fall directly on students, families, and institutions. Students are going to have to make hard decisions about whether they can go to college, stay in college. Folks are going to have to make hard decisions about how they're going to manage their student loans with the debt that they currently have. Parents are going to have to make hard decisions about whether they can afford to send their kids to school. Schools are going to have to make hard decisions about what programs they are able to keep, but some of them, whether they're even able to stay open with these changes. We should be very concerned. We know that there's an affordability crisis in higher education. We know that there's a student debt crisis and that is disproportionately burdening families of color, low-income students, veterans, women, all the folks who are disproportionately harmed when we make these huge cuts. This bill doesn't make life easier or make higher education more accessible for any of these communities. It puts it further out of reach.

So thank you. And my colleagues have talked a lot about eliminating the Department of Education, but I'm not sure the American people understand what the department actually does for students. So let me ask: Can you tell us what the Department of Education does for college students, for institutions of higher education? And can you talk about the negative impact that these layoffs, grant cancellations, interagency transfers have already had, especially on campuses trying to serve students? And how will the continuing dismantling of the department affect our most vulnerable students—low-income students, first-generation students, and students of color?

The Department of Education was created by statute by Congress, and one of its most important functions is that it protects the civil rights of students. Students are able, if they are being discriminated against on their campus, in their school district, anywhere, to to file complaints and to have that investigated by OCR, the Office for Civil Rights. But right now, because that department has been gutted, and that office specifically, thousands of complaints are going unanswered. Folks don't have a response. Last year alone, there were 23,000 complaints made to the Office for Civil Rights. Many of them are still open. Folks have submitted complaints this year. There is no continuity. They have no idea who their case officer is. There is no idea for next steps. And that impacts the schools and institutions as well. Many of them are waiting for guidance on what to do next. They're waiting on guidance on how to handle this. They're trying to do the right thing, but they don't even have anyone they can contact at the department.

So let me ask you about the dismantling of this department and the transfer or elimination of core programs and how it affects HBCUs' ability to serve their students and strengthen their campuses and continue their mission.

Anytime we try to move broad swaths of a program, we saw this already with the transfer of the Office of Career and Technical Education, there were disruptions in funding, disruptions in the system. All of this takes time to implement. It's not something that can be done overnight. We see this moving to departments where they don't have the expertise, the resources, the years of experience with these programs. And so there are going to be funding disruptions, and that will be most felt by the schools that are most under-resourced. Thank you.
very much, Mr. Chairman i yield back.
Thank you. I'd like to now recognize my friend from New York, Ms. Stefanik, who was actually a former member, a board member of Truman.

Thank you so much, Chairman Owens. Thank you for the witnesses for being here today. I've been tracking these issues quite closely and your work for some time, and most recently as a sitting board member of the foundation, and the first board meeting will be right after this hearing in about 5 minutes. I sent a letter to my fellow board members on May 28th of this year, raising serious concerns regarding the ideological bias and impartiality of the scholarship selection process. So, I have a few questions for some of the witnesses. Mr. Kissel, based on your work examining ideological issues in higher education, what are the inherent risks to a congressionally established scholarship program like the Truman Foundation when public reporting suggests its selection process may be prioritizing ideological alignment over the merits of leadership and public service?

Thank you for the question. Every government body can easily be captured by politics and ideology. Non-governmental bodies can as well. But the problem is especially acute for organizations like the Truman Program, where the members of the foundation are political members.

Thank you. Ms. Kabbany, do you believe that the foundation's current lack of transparency in its selection criteria and the makeup of its selection committees make it vulnerable to political and social activism rather than those committed to broad, nonpartisan public service?

Absolutely, that can have an impact on who they decide to send forward as the candidates and the fellows. Also, on the campus level, those that are deciding who gets put to the regional committees. I mean, they're professors, and we all know 30 to 1 professors are liberal, so they're obviously gonna advance candidates who have beliefs and pet causes that they love and they support and they wanna see funded. So the bias actually starts at the campus level and then goes to the regional and the final 2, so it's really systemic.

Thank you. Dr. Hess, I have questioned the will and commitment of the foundation's board to maintaining ideological neutrality. What specific actions or policy changes should the board and the foundation immediately implement to restore public trust and demonstrate a genuine commitment to political and ideological neutrality in their selections?

It's a great question. Look, and it's important for folks to understand why this matters so much. The Truman Fellowship exists as a model of how we want to encourage young Americans to engage in public service. We want young leaders who can model the breadth of good-faith disagreement in this country, who can bridge divides, who can lead us forward. We cannot do this if half of the nation is not is not at the table. So what kinds of changes are necessary? One, look, the Truman Program ought to understand its primary mission as making sure it is inviting all Americans to the table. It needs to recruit aggressively on campuses where it is not currently getting submissions. It needs to make sure it is reaching out to networks it may not have already tapped. There needs to be public transparency and scrutiny about the processes. Right now, the regional review boards, if you survey—as the chairman mentioned, if you survey the make up of the judges, it's pretty clear that there's a heavy ideological tilt. That needs to be addressed. There need to be clear guidelines on the kinds of questions that should and should not be asked in the interview process. Really, what we need is somebody to approach this with the primary goal of reassuring all Americans, all students, all professors, that we are trying to create a heterodox, inclusive community of scholars who can lead us forward, rather than one that happens to be responsive to orthodoxy on campus.

Well, thank you. That's one of my missions and one of the reasons that I requested for this position on the board, and I've been deeply concerned. One of the most egregious examples is there was a 2025 Truman Scholar who publicly espoused support for Hamas, a U.S.-designated foreign terrorist organization. As you know, I've been a leader in combating antisemitism in the higher education space, and we need to address this rise of antisemitism with some of the recipients of the Truman Scholarship Program. So thank you very much. Look forward to working with you to try to implement many of these policy reforms, and I yield back.
Thank you. I'd like now to recognize my friend from Georgia, Ms. McBath.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you to our witnesses for being with us today. I've already read your testimonies. Ms. Harrington, my father was president of the Illinois branch NAACP for over 20 years in Chicago, in Illinois, at the height of the civil rights movement. And I'm so glad to see you here today to continue the important work to help this country actually live up to its promise of liberty and justice for all people. That promise, despite being the culminating line of our Pledge of Allegiance, despite being recited by members of Congress in classrooms around the country every single day, is one that is increasingly under attack by my Republican colleagues in Congress and the White House. Time and time again, Republicans attempt to demonize programs that make people's lives better as politically biased, because they simply don't believe them to be an important role of our government. It isn't about evaluating these programs on their merits or the benefit that they provide. It's about trying to fulfill their narrow view of what the role of our Federal Government should be. It's about propping up the idea that their way of thinking is the only acceptable one, regardless of the outcomes of the policies that they support. They're so focused on those goals that they fail to see the benefits that the work of these scholars and other public servants provides to our country and actually for the world. It's why this administration would rather pay money to set food on fire and destroy it than to see it end up in the hands of hungry women and children. Wanting to represent your country on the largest stage in the, in order to share how your work makes this country a better place is not a progressive ideal. It's a uniquely American one. Wanting to lead in spaces like human rights, wanting to eradicate poverty at home and abroad so that all those that are made in God's image can live a decent and fulfilling life—these are not progressive or partisan ideals. These are the things that make millions of Americans take real pride in their lives every single day. It's what is supposed to make this country so special and better than others like it. It isn't just about where you were born or where you live. It's about what your country stands for, whether it's really fighting for the ideals or just talking about them out of convenience. Ms. Harrington, as you know, the Truman Foundation requires scholars to take a job in public service for at least 3 of the 7 years after their studies. This suggests the idea that the scholarship's focus on public service itself is the source of the misguided opinion that a disproportionate share of Truman Scholars are progressive. Can you please talk about how conservative attacks on the importance and the benefits of public service play a role in the makeup of Truman Scholarship recipients? And if you can do so quickly, I have such short time.

I think this is just an attack on, on dissent, and, and public service should have no ideology, as you mentioned. Um, and so with bipartisan, bipartisan Board of Trustees, bipartisan selection committee, bipartisan selection committee, this is— this— they have created a program that values people who are interested in public service, period. It's not about partisan identity, but they're also trying to do an attack on public service and dissent so that they can also impact the services that are provided by these entities. Right. And the communities that are impacted by these services. And so it's an idea of not just attacking the beliefs and ideologies, but what the— what hap— what, what organizations, governments can do for the communities they serve.

Thank you. So this is clearly just another episode of selective outrage over the use of public dollars. So let's put this in perspective. We are having a hearing today over an annual appropriation that's made by Congress of just $3 million. Just 3 million. An appropriation supported by Congress and signed into law by the president. President Trump just sent $20 billion, and that's billion with a B, to help his political allies in Argentina win a foreign election. And the Republican majority will not condemn that as a misuse of public funds. I don't believe any committee or subcommittee has had a hearing on that. Instead, we're using the people's time to examine $3 million specifically dedicated to scholarships meant for people trying to make this country a better and safer place to live. I don't believe this is a good use of this subcommittee or any subcommittee's time, and I hope that we recommit ourselves to real issues that have a positive impact on Americans' everyday lives. And I yield.
Thank you. And I'd like to recognize my friend from Wisconsin, Mr. Grothman.

Thank you very much. Ms. Kabbany, I found your testimony very interesting, particularly interesting given this is a public program. You mentioned that the people who run the program kind of scrubbed some information that you wanted and you couldn't really get all the information you wanted to adequately do the study. Could you comment on that a little bit and perhaps why the people who run the run the Truman Foundation want to hide things from Congress and the public?

Yes. So, I am aware that the biographies of the Truman winners have been removed. We started our research in 2015, and they used to publish everyone's biography, what nonprofits they were interested in, who they volunteered with, who they've interned with. And now when they publish the winners, they just give their name and their school. Yeah, just the name and the school. And so we've used LinkedIn bios and their social media accounts, and other school biographies or other public statements they've made. But, unfortunately, the Truman Foundation has made it a bit more difficult for us to do our research every year.

Okay, kind of that contempt for for the public. Okay, other couple comments. As far as the Argentina thing, I don't mean to get into that, but I believe it was a currency swap. It wasn't a guest, and at least as of a couple months ago, the US was ahead of the game in that. Do you guys know—one of you mentioned the already ideological bias that conservatives have to put up with from the faculty of the universities around the country. I think one of you threw out, but I'd like to repeat, what are the percentage of faculty in this country, particularly liberal arts faculty, that are kind of of the progressive bent?

Yeah, so, look, study after study shows that 30 to 1, 40 to 1 professors are liberal to conservative. And so whoever is tasked on these campuses with selecting the Truman fellows to nominate forward to the regional committees is probably a liberal, and they probably like liberal causes, progressive causes, Democratic causes. So it's really no surprise that the applicants that are moving forward lean left. So the problem starts on the campuses and whoever is selected on each campus to advance their school's nominee.

Okay. Ms. Harrington, when she talked, she mentioned that DEI was mentioned as a favorable thing. Is anybody familiar with where the DEI philosophy came from or familiar with Christopher Rufo's writings? You want to elaborate a little on who came up with DEI and what their ultimate goal is?

Critical theory started as a school of literary thought more than half a century ago. It was brought into particularly law as a way of pushing back on some of the assumptions of the US Constitution and of established federal law and state law.
What is the goal of labeling people by where their ancestors come from? From? Why is this so obsessed over today?
You know, I mean, I think there are obviously 2 schools of thought when it comes to equality. One is that Americans need to be equal under the law. A second is a philosophy of equity.
We'll give Jennifer one more question. What pushback has there been against the left turn from the Truman Foundation? Has there been pushback?

No, they essentially just say, Well, we can only field the players we're given. And so, okay, how do we reform the players they're given then? Because if we want to fix this and and create some balance, we need to advertise better on campuses to College Republicans and Turning Point USA and Young Americans for Freedom, and make sure that maybe the College of Business or the College of Economics, so that a wider net is cast and we get more applicants, and then make sure that the faculty who are selecting these candidates know that they need to put the best person forward, not just the one that mirrors what they believe.

Okay, Ms. Harrington, you want diversity. The country right now is about one-half Republican, one-half Democrat, about. Do you think it'd be a good goal for the Truman Foundation to have approximately one-half of their recipients more of a conservative bent and one-half more of a progressive bent?

I think the best goal for all programs, and particularly for this committee to focus on, is ensuring that we are taking down barriers and improving access for all. And that is the point of diversity, equity, inclusion, and access programs, which are help— which helps universities and will help this and will help institutions actually comply with their civil rights obligations and ensure that they're providing equal opportunity. So this is about taking down barriers and not continuing to put barriers up.
We know who the barriers are against, but in any event, thank you.
Thank you. I'd like now— excuse my— I have my And now it's my friend from Oregon, Ms. Bonamici.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member. I have to say, it's pretty disappointing and also pretty tone-deaf for the majority to use this committee's valuable time to talk about this politicized issue. I have been on this committee for more than a dozen years, and, Dr. Hess just talked about bridging divides, I can't remember a hearing that hasn't that has felt more divisive than this with these labels: left, right, conservative, liberal. My constituents back home aren't looking at labels. They want us to fix problems. They don't want us to label each other and label ideologies. And I have to say that Republicans want to talk about this scholarship program, but what we should be talking about is how we make higher education more affordable and accessible. We got the big ugly bill that wiped out federal support for student aid, the final rule on the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program now is subjecting public service workers to unfair political litmus tests and unnecessary limits on loan forgiveness. Let's talk about that. The administration is doing everything it can to undermine and shut down the Department of Education and the programs it administers that help students like TRIO and GEAR UP. Let's talk about the harmful and nonsensical declaration by the Trump administration that certain fields of study, including nursing, are no longer professional. Now it's going to make it harder for people to enter into this necessary and honorable work. And last week, the Department of Education announced another six interagency agreements are going to move several core functions to other agencies that are unequipped and underfunded and don't have the staff to operate these programs. This includes everything in the Office of Postsecondary Education, which administers critical higher education grant programs and technical assistance. And I want to ask you, Ms. Harrington, what's the role of the Office of Postsecondary Education in implementing higher education policy and overseeing student-centered grant programs? And what's at stake if students and colleges aren't able to access those services provided by the Office of Postsecondary Education in a timely manner?

It will be incredibly— it could be catastrophic. Their role is to not just determine who, who, how grants are awarded, to determine the, the qualifications. They work directly with institutions to implement the programs. They work directly with institutions to answer questions, to make sure that the programs are operating effectively, that they're getting to the students that they're supposed to get to, and evaluating their programs. So if you move them to another department that has no experience and doesn't have the staff to do this, then you're going to directly impact those institutions and their ability to carry out the programs and the students that relied on those programs. Which

is just closing the doors of opportunity to many. And Ms. Harrington, I trust we can agree that public service workers, like teachers, nurses, first responders, service members, those are critical jobs despite the low wages and understaffing. So the new Public Service Loan Forgiveness rule will continue the Trump administration's legacy of abandoning public service workers by allowing the Secretary to determine who's eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness based on political ideology, which is not what the country expects or needs. Public service workers deserve transparency in a system that works for them. Thank you, Chairman Owens and Ranking Member Adams. Thanks for hosting today's important hearing on Truman Scholarship Program, and since its inception, the program has provided critical financial support for students in the territories, including 27 scholars from Guam, 22 of which were from the University of Guam, which coincidentally established when Harry Truman was president. And the program has also supported an additional 75 students from the other territories and commonwealths. In comparison, other public service scholarships like Rhodes, Marshall, and Fulbright select far fewer, if any, awardees from the territories. Now, while college affordability is a problem everywhere, higher education costs and geographic barriers mean that it is especially challenging for students from Guam to access higher education. Receiving the Truman Scholarship can and has been transformational for students who receive it. So that is why I'm concerned to hear instances of political bias in federally funded program. This is the type of behavior that can threaten the program's long-term sustainability, and we must ensure that it is being administered fairly without regard for political affiliation, ensuring students across the political spectrum have a chance to succeed. From what I heard, the scholarship program can sometimes have limited outreach to programs that tend to have conservative students in them. What reforms can be made to ensure broader outreach and therefore greater intellectual and political diversity?

Thank you for the question. So, I think that we need to do better advertising and marketing to students who tend to go into those fields that you cited off, because $30,000 for grad school is $30,000 for grad school. I'm sure they wouldn't mind giving 3 years of a job of public service. Conservatives and Republicans love public service just as much as left-leaning students do, and it's a wonderful opportunity. A lot of times people have been saying, Well, it's only $3 million, but the Truman Scholarship fellows have an outsized role in advancing the national conversation. They go into jobs that are influencing lawmakers, that are influencing think tank policy papers, that are influencing all sorts of advocacy work. So, they're the cream of the crop of our students, and they're driven, they're ambitious, they're talented, and our right-leaning students deserve a fair shot at such a wonderful opportunity as much as the left-leaning students do.

Thank you, Mr. Hess. In your testimony, you touched on political bias problem with a specific focus on the awardees' political leanings. This seems to also indicate that there could be bias in some of the panels selecting finalists and winners. You mentioned this briefly in your written testimony, but did you also do research into political leaning of these panels? If so, what did you find?

I have not delved deeply into the makeup of the regional review boards. If one looks at the publicly available names and tries to identify their ideological leanings, it's roughly 4-to-1, left to right. I think it's useful to understand I've had a number of former Truman fellows and Truman board members reach out over the last year or so since I wrote this. And one former Truman board member explained that when this question comes up of why there are not more right-leaning folks involved in the program, there generally are two responses, he indicated. One was that, look, Republicans and conservatives just aren't interested in public service. That's why they're not here. They just don't want to be here. And the second is conservatives and Republicans are just not as academically accomplished. They're just not as credentialed. So they are losing out in a merit-based competition. Personally, having been a teacher, a professor, and a scholar at AEI for decades, I have not found either of those defenses to ring true.
Oh,
one last thing as a follow-up also. What steps might Congress be able to take to ensure balanced and fair representation on these review and award panels?

Honestly, I'm less concerned about representation than I am about fairness and merit. For instance, of the 182 awardees in the— between 2021 and 2023, just 4 looked at cybersecurity and technology. This says to me that the priorities of what judges are looking for and asking about are askew. And so I think what we need is careful scrutiny to ensure that it is public service in the national interest with an eye to forging inclusive, healthy conversation.
Thank you very much to the panel. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. You go back.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Yeah, I think this hearing is really part of an ideological agenda, taking a quote from Dr. Hess introduction speech. I have a concern in Arizona's CD-7. We have a lot of rural communities. Rural students and local colleges are already facing shrinking resources and limited access to higher education. It puts it— it puts college even further out of reach if they have fewer resources to go to school. The institutions themselves have fewer resources to provide services. And in rural communities, oftentimes these institutions, just like many others, are the drivers of that economy as well. And so if these institutions are struggling, the entire community struggles, and that will have ripple effects across that community.

Thank you. Ms. Kabbany, you mentioned left-leaning careers when you were talking about the kinds of your assessment. I'm wondering if an immigration attorney would be considered a left or right-leaning career.

That would probably fall under a could not classify or potentially left-leaning if that person also had other Democratic or progressive items on their bio so that we could make a better determination.

Uh, okay. Well, listen, today we're talking about a federally funded scholarship program for graduate degrees that honors the legacy of President Harry Truman. In my opinion, the federal government has no business running a scholarship program at all. And with our national debt over $38 trillion, which I just left a hearing where that conversation was being discussed, we literally cannot afford these luxury academic subsidies. In 2024, taxpayers spent $3 million to send about 60 people to graduate school through the Truman Scholarship. This is not the role envisioned by our founders, nor is it—we find it well outside our Constitution's limits. I don't fault any of the students. I certainly don't fault the alumni who've taken advantage of this program, because if the government offers free money, people will understandably accept it, but that does not make the program wise, nor does it make it justified. It simply means it is time for Congress to stop the gravy train. At a time when our nation is drowning in debt, every dollar must be scrutinized. The American people are calling for every dollar to be scrutinized, and for this reason, I believe we should no longer fund this program. And today's hearing, I think, if anything else, has exposed the liberal bias within the program, adding just one more reason we should not spend any more money on it. And with that, Mr. Chairman, I yield back my time.

There have been numerous studies that by not doing something about these barriers, by keeping people out of post-secondary education, by keeping them out of employment opportunities, for instance, we lose trillions of dollars to our economy, actually. And just in, in in general, young people go in to get a bachelor's degree to be special ed teachers. We need— now, they're not part of this right now, but moving that out of the Department of Education, which has been proposed as well, is there is a level of expertise in getting diverse groups, irrespective of their ideology, and different perspectives in society, poverty, but also specific needs in our education system. I think we believe in the value of public service, and so we support making sure that there are pathways for folks to go into public service, whether it be through the Truman Scholarship, through other programs. Folks who are just trying to go through grad school with regular federal student loans, regular federal grants, who have to navigate this complex system, this more expensive system that's being created by this big beautiful bill. And so what we are concerned about is how we make sure that more pathways are being created and not focusing on trying to close one small pathway.

Thank you. And I'd like to recognize chairman of the full committee, Chairman Walberg.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you for this hearing. Let's talk about what they're studying and whether it seems reflective of the kinds of issues that are important to this country and that reflect the broad swath of views and values of American college students and of the American taxpaying and voting public. They removed those. They also then went ahead and hid past press releases bragging about the winners so that only those with a Truman account can actually go back and look at this. So then, when they complain about the nature of the study, they complain about the study at the same time they've made it impossible for anybody to actually assess the virtue.

Yeah, except those they want to see the system. Okay, thank you. Ms. Kabbany, you mentioned that the Truman Foundation selects students from almost every state. Why has that practice failed to ensure that conservative students get a fair chance?

And so they're having a big influence on our nation's conversation and on what legislation is brought forth. This isn't just a $3 million scholarship. This is the direction of our country and those that are leading it. And so the problem needs to be reformed because it's absolutely not fair to 50% of American taxpayers.

Yeah. Yeah. And certainly it doesn't even come close to, in many states, the percentage of the makeup of the congressional delegation as well. And we're not asking for that, but we're asking for a fair approach to it. Thank you. Mr. Kissel, one downstream effect of Truman bias is that students at universities considered right-leaning are effectively disqualified, at least it appears, from competing for the award. And if you look at right-leaning or faith-based institutions, it's an extremely, extremely small number.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to all the witnesses for being here today. When Congress established the Truman Scholarship, it made this finding: Because of the desirability of encouraging young people to recognize that political— and provide service in the highest and best traditions of the American political system at all levels of government, it is especially appropriate to honor former President Harry S. included, so that we we see colleges taking more seriously: How do we reach out to folks who are not on campus? because another option is to zero it out.

and as has been testified, they worked hard at making sure you didn't have the information so you could make those findings.
